```{r, data-prep}
#| echo: false

data <- read_excel(here("data/Naplan_Results.xlsx"), sheet = 3, col_names = TRUE)
```

## The Dangers of Averages

Every year, over a million Australian kids sit down to the same NAPLAN tests, and every year the national headlines report more or less the same story: scores are steady, nothing much has changed. But national averages have a way of flattening out the most important parts of a story. Dig into who is actually sitting behind those averages, and a very different picture emerges -- one where an entire group of students is measurably and consistently being left behind. This post works through that data step by step: starting from the national numbers everyone sees, then preliminarily examining the data to pull apart who gets tested, who doesn't, and what the gap actually looks like once you stop averaging it away.

## Where Did the Data Come From?

NAPLAN tests Australian enrolled Year 3, 5, 7, and 9 students, though some are exempt (disability, recent arrival) or absent, so participation isn't 100%. Observations are aggregated statistics (mean, SD, CI, proficiency-band %) by year, domain, state, and subgroup, not individual student records. Variables cover performance, participation, and demographics. "NAPLAN Results" (sheet 3) is the key analysis sheet. Anonymisation relies on aggregation; flags suppress cells with under 30 assessed students (n.p.) or for policy reasons (s.p.) -- the latter resulted in Tasmania's omission, due to low participation.

## How Do the Scores Look?

For the sake of matching variables and observing educational effects, this report will only follow the performance of the 2026 Year 5 cohort. Before we dive too deeply, let us first establish a baseline of average performance across NAPLAN tests for these students. For readability, we will abbreviate the names of the domains: Writing (W), Reading (R), Spelling (S), Numeracy (N), and Grammar and Punctuation (GaP).

```{r, data-filter}
#| echo: false

domain_abbrev <- c(
  "Grammar and Punctuation" = "GaP",
  "Numeracy" = "N",
  "Reading" = "R",
  "Spelling" = "S",
  "Writing" = "W"
)

data_y5_2026_overall <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5,
  `Calendar year` == 2026,
  `Student attribute` == "All",
  `State/territory` == "Australia") |>
  mutate(highlight = case_when(
    `Average NAPLAN score` == max(`Average NAPLAN score`, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Highest",
    `Average NAPLAN score` == min(`Average NAPLAN score`, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Lowest",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  mutate(
    Domain = recode(Domain, !!!domain_abbrev),
    Domain = fct_reorder(Domain, `Average NAPLAN score`)
  )

# Domain order (by national average score) reused so facets in the
# state-level plot appear in the same order as the national summary
domain_levels <- levels(data_y5_2026_overall$Domain)

state_abbrev <- c(
  "Australia" = "AUS",
  "New South Wales" = "NSW",
  "Victoria" = "VIC",
  "Queensland" = "QLD",
  "South Australia" = "SA",
  "Western Australia" = "WA",
  "Tasmania" = "TAS",
  "Northern Territory" = "NT",
  "Australian Capital Territory" = "ACT"
)

# Order states by their average score across domains (ascending), so
# the state axis reflects performance rather than an arbitrary order
state_levels <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5,
  `Calendar year` == 2026,
  `Student attribute` == "All") |>
  mutate(state_abbrev = recode(`State/territory`, !!!state_abbrev)) |>
  summarise(mean_score = mean(`Average NAPLAN score`, na.rm = TRUE), .by = state_abbrev) |>
  # Tasmania's data is suppressed (s.p.), so it has no score to order by
  filter(!is.na(mean_score)) |>
  arrange(mean_score) |>
  pull(state_abbrev)

data_y5_2026 <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5,
  `Calendar year` == 2026,
  `Student attribute` == "All") |>
  mutate(
    state_abbrev = factor(recode(`State/territory`, !!!state_abbrev), levels = state_levels),
    Domain = factor(recode(Domain, !!!domain_abbrev), levels = domain_levels)
  ) |>
  # Tasmania's scores are suppressed (s.p.), so drop it rather than
  # plot an empty/NA state category
  filter(!is.na(state_abbrev)) |>
  # Rank within domain so highest/lowest state can be highlighted per facet
  mutate(
    highlight = case_when(
      `Average NAPLAN score` == max(`Average NAPLAN score`, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Highest",
      `Average NAPLAN score` == min(`Average NAPLAN score`, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "Lowest",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    .by = Domain
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-national-domain-summary
#| fig-cap: "National average NAPLAN score, with confidence interval, by domain (2026, Year 5). Tasmania is omitted, for missing data."

ggplot(data_y5_2026_overall, aes(x = Domain, y = `Average NAPLAN score`)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(
    ymin = `Average NAPLAN score` - `Average NAPLAN score confidence interval`,
    ymax = `Average NAPLAN score` + `Average NAPLAN score confidence interval`
  )) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

@fig-national-domain-summary shows that when aggregated nationally, there is not particularly significant difference in the average scoring across each of the domains assessed in NAPLAN, with a range of only 15 points between all domains. Grammar and Punctuation holds the highest average score (though also appears to be the most variable), while Writing holds the lowest average score.

```{r}
#| label: fig-state-domain-summary
#| fig-cap: "State average NAPLAN score, with confidence interval, by domain (2026, Year 5), offset horizontally within each domain to reduce overlap, coloured by state/territory. Tasmania is omitted, for missing data."

# Full 8-colour Okabe-Ito palette, chosen for maximum distinguishability
# under colour vision deficiency (more distinct than a viridis subset).
# Kept at 8 colours (matching all state_abbrev levels, including AUS)
# so each state's colour stays consistent even though AUS is dropped
# from this particular plot.
okabe_ito_8 <- c(
  "#000000", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73",
  "#F0E442", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7"
)

# Shared, deterministic dodge (rather than random jitter) so each
# state's line vertex lands exactly on its own point/error bar
dodge_pos <- position_dodge(width = 0.6)

data_y5_2026 |>
  # AUS is the national aggregate rather than a state/territory, so
  # it's excluded from this state-level plot only
  filter(state_abbrev != "AUS") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Domain, y = `Average NAPLAN score`, color = state_abbrev, group = state_abbrev)) +
  geom_line(position = dodge_pos) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(
    ymin = `Average NAPLAN score` - `Average NAPLAN score confidence interval`,
    ymax = `Average NAPLAN score` + `Average NAPLAN score confidence interval`
  ), position = dodge_pos, size = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito_8, drop = TRUE) +
  labs(color = "State/territory")
```

@fig-state-domain-summary shows the performance of each state across domains. Viewing this on a single plot exposes that Northern Territory trails the rest of the states/territories by a wide margin across every domain. While the remaining states cluster fairly closely together, with rank order shifting slightly between domains. Additionally, NT is shown to have the largest confidence intervals, suggesting a greater range in their scores and the possibility of an even lower "true" average.

```{r}
#| label: fig-state-domain-diff
#| fig-cap: "Each state's average NAPLAN score minus the AUS average for that domain (2026, Year 5), offset horizontally within each domain to reduce overlap, coloured by state/territory. Tasmania is omitted, for missing data. Error bars combine each state's confidence interval with the national reference's confidence interval in quadrature (treating the two as independent), so they reflect uncertainty in both terms of the difference."

data_y5_2026_diff <- data_y5_2026 |>
  mutate(
    aus_score = `Average NAPLAN score`[state_abbrev == "AUS"],
    aus_ci = `Average NAPLAN score confidence interval`[state_abbrev == "AUS"],
    diff = `Average NAPLAN score` - aus_score,
    # Combine the state's and AUS's CIs in quadrature, treating them as
    # independent margins of error (each is reported as ~1.96 * SE, so
    # this is equivalent to summing variances then rescaling)
    diff_ci = sqrt(`Average NAPLAN score confidence interval`^2 + aus_ci^2),
    .by = Domain
  ) |>
  filter(state_abbrev != "AUS")

ggplot(data_y5_2026_diff, aes(x = Domain, y = diff, color = state_abbrev, group = state_abbrev)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(position = dodge_pos) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(
    ymin = diff - diff_ci,
    ymax = diff + diff_ci
  ), position = dodge_pos, size = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito_8, drop = TRUE) +
  # Wrapped and shrunk since the full title was clipped at the top of
  # this tall, narrow (aspect.ratio = 1) plot
  labs(y = "Difference from AUS\naverage NAPLAN score", color = "State/territory") +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11))
```

@fig-state-domain-diff re-centres @fig-state-domain-summary on the national average, which makes clearer that NT sits roughly 70-85 points below the national average across every domain -- an order of magnitude larger than the spread among the remaining states/territories (all within about ±10 points of the national average). Note that the error bars combine each state's and AUS's confidence intervals in quadrature, assuming independence. But the two are not strictly independent since the AUS aggregate is computed by pooling all states, including the one being compared; this likely makes the error bars somewhat conservative (wider than the true uncertainty).

Cumulatively, these figures suggest that there is some disparity in performance between the Northern Territory and other states. Let us dive deeper into what might be driving this...

## Who is Doing the Tests?

Now, we know the average scores aren't consistent across all states. But could there be other factors skewing our picture of performance?

```{r, participation-subgroups-prep}
#| echo: false

demo_data <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5,
         `Calendar year` == 2026,
         `State/territory` == "Australia",
         `Student attribute` != "All") |>
  summarise(
    `Participation (%)` = mean(`Participation (%)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Average NAPLAN score` = mean(`Average NAPLAN score`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(`Student attribute`, Subgroup)
  )

# Abbreviated/wrapped facet strip labels so labels aren't truncated in
# the narrow per-attribute columns below (columns with only 2-5
# subgroups, like Gender or Indigeneity, are especially tight since
# column width is proportional to the number of subgroups)
attribute_abbrev <- c(
  "ABS remoteness" = "Remote.",
  "Gender" = "Gender",
  "Indigeneity" = "Indig.",
  "Indigeneity by ABS remoteness" = "Indig. x\nRemote.",
  "Language background" = "Lang.",
  "Parental education" = "Parent.\nEduc.",
  "Parental occupation" = "Parent.\nOccup."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-participation-subgroups
#| fig-cap: "Participation rate versus average NAPLAN score across all demographic subgroups (2026, Year 5, national, averaged across domains), coloured by average score. Subgroups (x-axis) are grouped by demographic attribute (facet columns, sorted by participation rate within each), motivating a closer look at Indigeneity and ABS remoteness in the rest of this section."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

demo_data |>
  mutate(Subgroup = fct_reorder(Subgroup, `Participation (%)`)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Subgroup, y = `Participation (%)`, color = `Average NAPLAN score`)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(`Student attribute`), scales = "free_x", space = "free_x",
             labeller = labeller(`Student attribute` = attribute_abbrev)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8, angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1),
    strip.text.x = element_text(size = 6),
    aspect.ratio = NULL
  )
```

@fig-participation-subgroups depicts test participation across different demographic subgroups. The lowest-participation subgroups across the whole dataset are concentrated in remoteness, Indigeneity and their intersection. While other demographic splits (gender, language background, parental education/occupation) stay within a, relatively, much narrower, higher-participation range. As such, the remainder of this section drills into Indigeneity by ABS remoteness.

```{r, participation-prep}
#| echo: false

# National overall average score (across domains), used as the
# reference point for the colour scale below
aus_avg_score <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5,
         `Calendar year` == 2026,
         `State/territory` == "Australia",
         `Student attribute` == "All") |>
  summarise(`Average NAPLAN score` = mean(`Average NAPLAN score`, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(`Average NAPLAN score`)

indig_remote <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5,
         `Calendar year` == 2026,
         `State/territory` == "Australia",
         `Student attribute` == "Indigeneity by ABS remoteness") |>
  summarise(
    `Participation (%)` = mean(`Participation (%)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Average NAPLAN score` = mean(`Average NAPLAN score`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Subgroup
  ) |>
  mutate(
    indigeneity = if_else(str_detect(Subgroup, "^Non-Indigenous"), "Non-Indigenous", "Indigenous"),
    # Match the shape/legend order used in the earlier version of this plot
    indigeneity = factor(indigeneity, levels = c("Indigenous", "Non-Indigenous")),
    remoteness = str_remove(Subgroup, "^(Indigenous|Non-Indigenous) "),
    remoteness = str_to_sentence(remoteness),
    remoteness = factor(remoteness, levels = c("Major cities", "Inner regional", "Outer regional", "Remote", "Very remote")),
    # Order the x-axis by actual participation rate, rather than
    # alphabetically or by the fixed remoteness category order
    remoteness = fct_reorder(remoteness, `Participation (%)`, .fun = mean),
    diff = `Average NAPLAN score` - aus_avg_score
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-participation-diff
#| fig-cap: "Participation rate by Indigeneity and ABS remoteness (2026, Year 5, national), coloured by each subgroup's average NAPLAN score relative to the national overall average, with a line connecting the Indigenous and Non-Indigenous point at each remoteness level. Remoteness categories are ordered by average participation rate."

ggplot(indig_remote, aes(x = remoteness, y = `Participation (%)`)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = remoteness), color = "grey60") +
  # Black-outlined fillable shapes (21/22) stay visible even when the
  # fill colour is close to white, near the middle of the diverging scale
  geom_point(aes(fill = diff, shape = indigeneity), size = 4, color = "black", stroke = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#D55E00", mid = "white", high = "#0072B2", midpoint = 0) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(Indigenous = 21, `Non-Indigenous` = 22)) +
  labs(x = "ABS remoteness", shape = NULL, fill = "Difference from AUS\nAverage NAPLAN Score") +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(order = 1), fill = guide_colorbar(order = 2)) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1), aspect.ratio = NULL)
```

@fig-participation-diff zooms in on the relationship between Indigeneity, remoteness, participation rates and deviation from national overall average NAPLAN scores. This simultaneously highlights the positive relationship between participation and impact on score (likely suggesting that areas with greater access to testing are also more likely to have greater educational resources), and the negative relationship between remoteness and participation. This also exposes the major gaps in participation rates between Indigenous and Non-Indigenous students, particularly in more remote areas. But, perhaps most importantly, this highlights our most vulnerable and lowest-performing test-takers: the Very remote Indigenous students.

It is interesting to note that this gap shrinks with lesser remoteness (though the reason for this will be explained with the next figure).

```{r, participation-prep-states}
#| echo: false

indig_remote_states <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5,
         `Calendar year` == 2026,
         `Student attribute` == "Indigeneity by ABS remoteness") |>
  mutate(
    state_abbrev = factor(recode(`State/territory`, !!!state_abbrev), levels = state_levels)
  ) |>
  # Tasmania is suppressed (s.p.) and AUS is the national aggregate
  # already shown in fig-participation-score/-diff, so both are excluded
  filter(!is.na(state_abbrev), state_abbrev != "AUS") |>
  summarise(
    `Participation (%)` = mean(`Participation (%)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Average NAPLAN score` = mean(`Average NAPLAN score`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(state_abbrev, Subgroup)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    indigeneity = if_else(str_detect(Subgroup, "^Non-Indigenous"), "Non-Indigenous", "Indigenous"),
    indigeneity = factor(indigeneity, levels = c("Indigenous", "Non-Indigenous")),
    remoteness = str_remove(Subgroup, "^(Indigenous|Non-Indigenous) "),
    remoteness = str_to_sentence(remoteness),
    # Reuse the national plot's remoteness order so the x-axis is
    # consistent across every state facet
    remoteness = factor(remoteness, levels = levels(indig_remote$remoteness)),
    diff = `Average NAPLAN score` - aus_avg_score
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-participation-heatmap-states
#| fig-cap: "Participation rate (tile colour) and average NAPLAN score relative to the national overall average (numeric label) by Indigeneity, ABS remoteness, and state/territory (2026, Year 5). Grey tiles are either suppressed (n.p., fewer than 30 students assessed) or a remoteness category that doesn't exist in that state. AUS and Tasmania are omitted (national aggregate and missing data, respectively)."

# Combines both variables from fig-participation-diff-states into a
# single compact grid: fill = participation rate, label = score
# difference from the AUS average. Label colour switches to white on
# darker (lower-participation) tiles so it stays legible throughout.
remoteness_abbrev <- c(
  "Very remote" = "Very remote",
  "Remote" = "Remote",
  "Outer regional" = "Outer reg.",
  "Inner regional" = "Inner reg.",
  "Major cities" = "Major cities"
)

ggplot(indig_remote_states, aes(x = remoteness, y = state_abbrev, fill = `Participation (%)`)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(diff), color = `Participation (%)` > 75), size = 2.8, na.rm = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ indigeneity) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "white")) +
  # Abbreviating the two longest labels and using a gentler angle
  # keeps the x-axis text compact and legible
  scale_x_discrete(labels = remoteness_abbrev) +
  labs(x = "ABS remoteness", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1, size = 8), aspect.ratio = NULL)
```

And with @fig-participation-heatmap-states, we arrive at a clearer picture of who is performing how, and where. As expected from @fig-participation-diff, students who are Indigenous and Very remote consistently exhibit the weakest performance in their cohort. Adding this back to the state differences explored back in @fig-state-domain-diff, we see that Very remote, Indigenous students in NT are disproportionately disadvantaged, among the least likely to complete NAPLAN, and likely to receive the lowest score on average.

Answering the shrinking participation gap question raised by @fig-participation-diff, NT only contains observations that are "outer regional" or more remote, while also containing the lowest participation rates among Indigenous students. This would be massively down-weighting the estimate. Simultaneously, NT's absence from the more urban subgroups may be part of why these areas report lesser difference in participation, irrespective of Indigeneity.

It should also be noted that, while being suppressed from displaying score performance -- remote Victoria (irrespective of Indigeneity) and inner-regional ACT (specifically non-Indigenous) report perfect participation rates. This stands out from the surrounding data and may be worth investigating for entry validity.

## Are We ***All***  Learning as We Grow?

Now let's take a look at how our cohort has grown since we last saw them sit NAPLAN in Year 3, back in 2024.

```{r, cohort-gain-prep}
#| echo: false

cohort_gain <- read_excel(here("data/Naplan_Results.xlsx"), sheet = "Cohort gain", col_names = TRUE)

cohort_gain_national <- cohort_gain |>
  filter(`State/territory` == "Australia", `Student attribute` == "All") |>
  mutate(
    transition = paste0("Y", `Base year level`, "\u2192Y", `Year level`),
    transition = factor(transition, levels = c("Y3\u2192Y5", "Y5\u2192Y7", "Y7\u2192Y9")),
    cohort = paste0(`Base calendar year`, "\u2013", `Calendar year`),
    Domain = recode(Domain, !!!domain_abbrev)
  )

# Order domains by growth (score gain) for the Year 3 2024 -> Year 5
# 2026 cohort, reused across all Question 4 figures for consistency
growth_levels <- cohort_gain_national |>
  filter(transition == "Y3\u2192Y5", cohort == "2024\u20132026") |>
  arrange(Difference) |>
  pull(Domain)

cohort_gain_national <- cohort_gain_national |>
  mutate(Domain = factor(Domain, levels = growth_levels))

cohort_gain_states <- cohort_gain |>
  filter(`Student attribute` == "All") |>
  mutate(
    state_abbrev = factor(recode(`State/territory`, !!!state_abbrev), levels = state_levels)
  ) |>
  # AUS is shown separately in fig-cohort-gain; Tasmania's cohort gain
  # is entirely suppressed (s.p.), so both are excluded here
  filter(!is.na(state_abbrev), state_abbrev != "AUS", !is.na(Difference)) |>
  mutate(
    transition = paste0("Y", `Base year level`, "\u2192Y", `Year level`),
    transition = factor(transition, levels = c("Y3\u2192Y5", "Y5\u2192Y7", "Y7\u2192Y9")),
    # Shortened transition labels avoid axis text overlap across the
    # seven-panel facet grid
    transition_short = case_when(
      transition == "Y3\u2192Y5" ~ "3\u21925",
      transition == "Y5\u2192Y7" ~ "5\u21927",
      transition == "Y7\u2192Y9" ~ "7\u21929"
    ),
    transition_short = factor(transition_short, levels = c("3\u21925", "5\u21927", "7\u21929")),
    cohort = paste0(`Base calendar year`, "\u2013", `Calendar year`),
    Domain = factor(recode(Domain, !!!domain_abbrev), levels = growth_levels)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cohort-gain
#| fig-cap: "Average NAPLAN score gain by domain (national), for the single cohort of students who were in Year 3 in 2024 and Year 5 in 2026. Domains are ordered by growth (score gain), ascending."

# Restricted to the one cohort that was in Year 5 in 2026 (i.e. Year 3
# in 2024), matching the scope used in fig-cohort-gain-states and
# fig-cohort-gain-indig-remote
cohort_gain_national_y5_2026 <- cohort_gain_national |>
  filter(transition == "Y3\u2192Y5", cohort == "2024\u20132026")

ggplot(cohort_gain_national_y5_2026, aes(x = Domain, y = Difference)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Domain", y = "Score gain (Year 3 2024 \u2192 Year 5 2026)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

@fig-cohort-gain shows the aggregate national average growth in student scores between Year 3 and Year 5. From this, we learn that Writing not only is the lowest-scoring domain (as seen in @fig-national-domain-summary) but also the lowest-growth (~66 points). The other four domains exhibit comparably clustered growth between the two test attempts (~83-90 points). 

But does this hold up everywhere and for all types of students?

```{r}
#| label: fig-cohort-gain-states-raw
#| fig-cap: "Average NAPLAN score gain by domain and state/territory, for the single cohort of students who were in Year 3 in 2024 and Year 5 in 2026. Domains are ordered by growth (score gain), ascending, as in @fig-cohort-gain. AUS is omitted (shown separately in @fig-cohort-gain) and Tasmania is omitted for missing data."

# Restricted to the one cohort that was in Year 5 in 2026 (i.e. Year 3
# in 2024); since only one transition exists for this cohort, the
# x-axis becomes domain rather than transition stage
cohort_gain_states_y5_2026 <- cohort_gain_states |>
  filter(transition == "Y3\u2192Y5", cohort == "2024\u20132026")

# All states combined onto one plot (as in fig-state-domain-jitter),
# using the same deterministic dodge so connecting lines land exactly
# on their points, rather than faceting into separate panels per state
ggplot(cohort_gain_states_y5_2026, aes(x = Domain, y = Difference, color = state_abbrev, group = state_abbrev)) +
  geom_line(position = dodge_pos, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(position = dodge_pos, size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito_8[1:7]) +
  labs(x = "Domain", y = "Score gain (Year 3 2024 \u2192 Year 5 2026)", color = "State/territory") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = NULL)
```

@fig-cohort-gain-states-raw shows that Writing remains the weakest growth area across all states, maintaining the clustered shape for the other four domains. Notably, however, NT trumps other states for growth in Reading and Spelling scores. Though, given the scores remain relatively low post-growth, this is realistically just weak convergence to mean performance.

Shifting our focus back to subgroups -- how do Indigenous students fare at the state level?

```{r}
#| label: fig-cohort-gain-states
#| fig-cap: "Gap in average NAPLAN score growth between Indigenous and Non-Indigenous students (Indigenous minus Non-Indigenous), by domain and state/territory, for the single cohort of students who were in Year 3 in 2024 and Year 5 in 2026. The Cohort gain sheet does not report Indigeneity broken down by state, so gain is reconstructed here directly from the main NAPLAN Results sheet (Year 5 2026 score minus Year 3 2024 score, per domain/state/Indigeneity). Domains are ordered by growth (score gain), ascending, as in @fig-cohort-gain. AUS is omitted (shown separately) and Tasmania is omitted for missing data. Positive values mean Indigenous students gained more than Non-Indigenous students in that domain/state."

cohort_indig_states <- data |>
  filter(`Student attribute` == "Indigeneity",
         (`Year level` == 3 & `Calendar year` == 2024) | (`Year level` == 5 & `Calendar year` == 2026)) |>
  mutate(
    state_abbrev = factor(recode(`State/territory`, !!!state_abbrev), levels = state_levels)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(state_abbrev), state_abbrev != "AUS") |>
  mutate(
    point = if_else(`Year level` == 3, "Y3_2024", "Y5_2026"),
    Domain = factor(recode(Domain, !!!domain_abbrev), levels = growth_levels)
  ) |>
  select(Domain, state_abbrev, Subgroup, point, `Average NAPLAN score`) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = point, values_from = `Average NAPLAN score`) |>
  mutate(Difference = Y5_2026 - Y3_2024)

growth_gap_states <- cohort_indig_states |>
  select(Domain, state_abbrev, Subgroup, Difference) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Subgroup, values_from = Difference) |>
  mutate(gap = Indigenous - `Non-Indigenous`)

# All states combined onto one plot (as in fig-state-domain-jitter),
# using the same deterministic dodge so connecting lines land exactly
# on their points, rather than faceting into separate panels per state
ggplot(growth_gap_states, aes(x = Domain, y = gap, color = state_abbrev, group = state_abbrev)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(position = dodge_pos, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(position = dodge_pos, size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito_8[1:7]) +
  labs(x = "Domain", y = "Indigenous minus\nNon-Indigenous growth (points)", color = "State/territory") +
  theme(aspect.ratio = NULL, axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11))
```

Breaking things down by Indigeneity and state, @fig-cohort-gain-states shows that Reading and Spelling growth consistently favours Indigenous students across almost every state, while Writing and Numeracy consistently favour Non-Indigenous students. This is the same domain pattern seen nationally in @fig-cohort-gain. NT stands out as the state where this gap is smallest and most inconsistent, sitting closest to zero in most domains, while ACT shows the largest single gap (Reading, +26 points).

In a vacuum (like for NT in @fig-cohort-gain-states-raw) this would paint an optimistic picture for Indigenous students. However, even with these growths, the earlier figures show that the cohort's overall performance continues to lag well behind the national average.

So what does this all mean?

## Unmasking the Inequity

Well, let's revisit the plot from which this journey began, but now disaggregating scores by Indigeneity.

```{r, indigeneity-domain-prep}
#| echo: false

indig_domain <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5, `Calendar year` == 2026, `State/territory` == "Australia",
         `Student attribute` == "Indigeneity") |>
  mutate(Domain = factor(recode(Domain, !!!domain_abbrev), levels = domain_levels)) |>
  select(Domain, Subgroup, `Average NAPLAN score`)

national_baseline <- data_y5_2026_overall |>
  mutate(Domain = factor(Domain, levels = domain_levels)) |>
  mutate(Subgroup = "National average") |>
  select(Domain, Subgroup, `Average NAPLAN score`)

indig_domain_combined <- bind_rows(indig_domain, national_baseline) |>
  mutate(Subgroup = factor(Subgroup, levels = c("Indigenous", "National average", "Non-Indigenous")))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-indigeneity-domain
#| fig-cap: "Average NAPLAN score by domain (2026, Year 5, national), for Indigenous and Non-Indigenous students, alongside the overall national average as a baseline."

ggplot(indig_domain_combined, aes(x = Domain, y = `Average NAPLAN score`, color = Subgroup, group = Subgroup, linetype = Subgroup)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Indigenous = "#D55E00", `Non-Indigenous` = "#0072B2", `National average` = "grey40")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Indigenous = "solid", `Non-Indigenous` = "solid", `National average` = "dashed")) +
  labs(x = "Domain", y = "Average NAPLAN score", color = NULL, linetype = NULL)
```

As feared, @fig-indigeneity-domain reveals that the national average scores are actually masking Indigenous Australian performance; they only really paint a picture of the non-Indigenous students. This leaves a very vulnerable minority who is poorly represented in educational efforts and whose success is quite possibly being let down by the system.

And this is all, so far, just looking at aggregates and averages. How does this hold up at the performance band distribution level?

```{r, performance-band-prep}
#| echo: false

band_colors <- c(
  "Needs additional support" = "#D55E00",
  "Developing" = "#E69F00",
  "Strong" = "#56B4E9",
  "Exceeding" = "#0072B2"
)

band_data <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5, `Calendar year` == 2026, `State/territory` == "Australia",
         `Student attribute` == "Indigeneity") |>
  select(Domain, Subgroup, `Needs additional support (%)`, `Developing (%)`, `Strong (%)`, `Exceeding (%)`) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(`Needs additional support (%)`, `Developing (%)`, `Strong (%)`, `Exceeding (%)`),
               names_to = "band", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(
    band = str_remove(band, " \\(%\\)"),
    band = factor(band, levels = c("Needs additional support", "Developing", "Strong", "Exceeding")),
    Domain = factor(recode(Domain, !!!domain_abbrev), levels = growth_levels)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-performance-bands
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of students across NAPLAN performance bands (2026, Year 5, national), by domain and Indigeneity."

ggplot(band_data, aes(x = Subgroup, y = pct, fill = band)) +
  # reverse = TRUE stacks bars bottom-to-top in the order the band
  # factor levels are listed (Needs additional support ... Exceeding)
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Domain, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = band_colors) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(Indigenous = "Indig.", `Non-Indigenous` = "Non-Indig.")) +
  labs(x = "Indigeneity", y = "Students (%)", fill = "Performance band") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), aspect.ratio = NULL)
```

@fig-performance-bands confirms the gap seen in @fig-indigeneity-domain is not just a shift in the average, but a genuine redistribution across the whole performance spectrum. In every domain, Indigenous students are far more concentrated in "Needs additional support" (roughly 3-4 times the share of Non-Indigenous students) and far less represented in "Exceeding" (often less than a fifth the share). This is most pronounced in Grammar and Punctuation, where "Needs additional support" accounts for over 40% of Indigenous students, compared to under 10% of Non-Indigenous students.

Filtering this down even further, to our most vulnerable remote and Indigenous students, the story becomes even starker.

```{r, performance-bands-remote-prep}
#| echo: false

band_data_remote <- data |>
  filter(`Year level` == 5, `Calendar year` == 2026, `State/territory` == "Australia",
         `Student attribute` == "Indigeneity by ABS remoteness") |>
  mutate(
    indigeneity = if_else(str_detect(Subgroup, "^Non-Indigenous"), "Non-Indigenous", "Indigenous"),
    indigeneity = factor(indigeneity, levels = c("Indigenous", "Non-Indigenous")),
    remoteness = str_remove(Subgroup, "^(Indigenous|Non-Indigenous) "),
    remoteness = str_to_sentence(remoteness)
  ) |>
  filter(remoteness %in% c("Remote", "Very remote")) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(`Needs additional support (%)`, `Developing (%)`, `Strong (%)`, `Exceeding (%)`),
               names_to = "band", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(
    band = str_remove(band, " \\(%\\)"),
    band = factor(band, levels = c("Needs additional support", "Developing", "Strong", "Exceeding")),
    Domain = factor(recode(Domain, !!!domain_abbrev), levels = growth_levels),
    # Weight each remoteness category's band % by its enrolled student
    # count when aggregating, since Remote and Very remote have very
    # different population sizes
    n_students = pct / 100 * `Enrolled students`
  ) |>
  summarise(
    pct = 100 * sum(n_students) / sum(`Enrolled students`),
    .by = c(Domain, indigeneity, band)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-performance-bands-remote
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of students across NAPLAN performance bands (2026, Year 5, national), by domain and Indigeneity, for Remote and Very remote areas combined (weighted by enrolled students)."

ggplot(band_data_remote, aes(x = indigeneity, y = pct, fill = band)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Domain, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = band_colors) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(Indigenous = "Indig.", `Non-Indigenous` = "Non-Indig.")) +
  labs(x = "Indigeneity", y = "Students (%)", fill = "Performance band") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), aspect.ratio = NULL)
```

@fig-performance-bands-remote shows the disparity amplifies sharply in remote areas: across Remote and Very remote areas combined, 60-74% of Indigenous students fall into "Needs additional support" depending on domain, compared to roughly 10-19% of Non-Indigenous students in the same areas, and "Exceeding" is almost entirely absent for Indigenous students (under 1% in every domain).

The performance band's name is fitting: these kids need additional support. We cannot keep ignoring this disparity. ***We cannot continue to leave our Indigenous youth behind.***

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## TL;DR

Nationally, NAPLAN scores look fairly consistent across domains and states -- until the Northern Territory and Indigenous students are considered on their own. NT trails every other state by a wide margin, driven largely by its Very remote Indigenous population, who also have the lowest participation rates in the country. Disaggregating by Indigeneity shows the national average has been masking this gap all along: Indigenous students are several times more likely to fall into "Needs additional support" performance bands when compared to their non-Indigenous counterparts, and are almost entirely absent from "Exceeding," with the disparity most severe in remote areas. Growth between Year 3 and Year 5 doesn't close this gap either. The data points to one conclusion: Indigenous students, especially in remote communities, are being systemically left behind by the current system. More investigation and focus is needed to address this systemic issue and ensure equitable access and outcomes for all students.
:::
